title: Jesus Seated at the Right Hand of the Father
paragraphs:
Jesus Seated at the Right Hand of the Father
If Jesus and the Father Are One, Why Is Jesus Sitting Beside Him?
There are moments in Scripture that seem simple until you stare at them long enough.
Jesus ascends into heaven.
The disciples watch.
The clouds receive Him.
And then Scripture repeatedly tells us something astonishing:
"He sat down at the right hand of God."
For many believers, that single statement creates an uncomfortable question.
If Jesus is God...
If Jesus said, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30)...
Why is Jesus sitting next to the Father?
Is there one throne or two?
One God or two?
One divine person or two separate beings?
For centuries skeptics have pointed to this verse as evidence that Christianity contradicts itself.
But the deeper you go into Scripture, the more breathtaking the answer becomes.
This is not a contradiction.
It is one of the most beautiful revelations of the Gospel.
And once you understand it, you will never read the Ascension the same way again.
Imagine a son returning home after winning a war.
His clothes are stained.
His hands bear scars.
The battle is finished.
The enemy has been defeated.
The kingdom is secure.
The father stands waiting.
Then the son walks into the throne room and takes the seat of honor beside his father.
Not because he is less than his father.
Not because he is a different king.
But because the victory has been completed.
This is the picture the New Testament paints of Jesus.
The phrase "right hand" is not primarily about geography.
It is about authority.
Power.
Honor.
Kingship.
Dominion.
In Hebrew thought, the right hand symbolized supreme authority.
The Hebrew word is:
יָמִין (yamin)
It literally means "right hand," but throughout the Old Testament it became a symbol of power, strength, favor, and royal authority.
David writes:
The Psalmist declares:
"The LORD says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool." (Psalm 110:1)
The Hebrew text reads:

נְאֻם יְהוָה לַאדֹנִי שֵׁב לִימִינִי
(Ne'um YHWH l'Adoni, shev limini)
"The LORD said to my Lord, sit at My right hand."
This became the most quoted Old Testament passage in the entire New Testament.
Not because early Christians were obsessed with seating arrangements in heaven.
Because they understood what it meant.
Jesus had been publicly enthroned.
Then comes the Greek New Testament.
After His resurrection, Mark records:
"The Lord Jesus, after He had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God." (Mark 16:19)
The Greek reads:

ἐκάθισεν ἐκ δεξιῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ
(ekathisen ek dexiōn tou Theou)
"Sat down at the right hand of God."
The phrase ἐκ δεξιῶν (ek dexiōn) means the position of highest honor and authority.
Not a second throne competing with God's throne.
The place of shared rule.
Shared dominion.
Shared glory.
Now comes the question that changes everything.
If Jesus is seated at the Father's right hand...
Are there two Gods?
Scripture answers with a thunderous no.
Israel's foundational confession remains true:

שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל
(Shema Yisrael)
"Hear, O Israel."

יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד
(YHWH Eloheinu YHWH Echad)
"The LORD our God, the LORD is One." (Deuteronomy 6:4)
The key word is:
אֶחָד (echad)
One.
But not necessarily solitary.
The same word is used when:
"The two shall become one flesh."
A husband and wife remain distinct persons.
Yet they are one.
United.
Perfectly joined.
The Father and the Son are distinct Persons.
Yet one divine essence.
One God.
Not two gods sharing power.
One God revealed as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Jesus Himself explained this mystery.
In John 17:5 He prayed:
"Father, glorify Me in Your own presence with the glory that I had with You before the world existed."
Notice what He did not say.
He did not ask for a new glory.
He asked for the glory He already possessed before creation.
Before Bethlehem.
Before the manger.
Before humanity existed.
The Son eternally shared the Father's glory.
This is why John opens his Gospel:
"In the beginning was the Word."
The Greek:

Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος
(En archē ēn ho Logos)
"And the Word was with God."

καὶ ὁ Λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν Θεόν
(kai ho Logos ēn pros ton Theon)
The phrase πρὸς τὸν Θεόν (pros ton Theon) implies intimate face-to-face fellowship.
Distinct Person.
Yet then John immediately adds:

καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ Λόγος
(kai Theos ēn ho Logos)
"And the Word was God."
Not merely godlike.
Not a lesser deity.
God Himself.
Distinct from the Father.
Yet fully divine.
Then something extraordinary happens after the resurrection.
For the first time in history, a glorified human body enters heaven.
Jesus remains fully God.
But He is also forever fully human.
The scars remain.
The resurrected body remains.
The humanity remains.
The Son who became flesh returns to heaven as the God-Man.
This is why Hebrews says:
"After making purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high." (Hebrews 1:3)
Priests in the Old Testament never sat down.
Their work was never finished.
Sacrifices continued endlessly.
But Jesus offered one perfect sacrifice.
Then He sat down.
Not because He was tired.
Because redemption was complete.
The cross worked.
The debt was paid.
The victory was won.
Stephen saw this reality moments before his martyrdom.
As stones crushed his body, heaven opened.
He cried:
"I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God." (Acts 7:56)
Notice something remarkable.
Most passages show Jesus seated.
Stephen sees Him standing.
Almost as if heaven itself rose to welcome its faithful witness home.
The King stood for His servant.
Even in death, Stephen was not abandoned.
So what does Jesus sitting at the Father's right hand mean?
It means He reigns.
It means His sacrifice succeeded.
It means His authority is absolute.
It means the crucified Savior is now the enthroned King.
It means the One who wore a crown of thorns now wears many crowns.
It means the One who was mocked now rules the universe.
It means the One who stretched out His hands on a cross now holds history in those same scarred hands.
And perhaps most beautifully...
It means humanity already has a representative in heaven.
A glorified man sits on the throne.
Jesus did not merely open the door to heaven.
He carried our humanity into the very presence of God.
Maybe that is what makes this truth so personal.
Because many believers imagine Jesus as a distant figure somewhere beyond the stars.
But Scripture presents something far more intimate.
The One seated at the Father's right hand still bears the wounds that purchased your salvation.
The King remembers the nails.
The scars remain visible.
The throne has not erased His love.
The crown has not erased His compassion.
The glory has not erased the cross.
The One ruling heaven is still the Lamb who was slain.
And that means the heart that bled for you is the same heart reigning over eternity.
What part of Christ's exaltation moves you most?
Your testimony may strengthen someone silently scrolling through their darkest season.
And never forget this:
The hands that were pierced for you now hold the scepter of the universe.
